status: Both new photographs await John’s review.

scout.source_use: Foreground Brussels sprout, its timber stake and the camera framing. Existing blue row lashings provide context. The mallet and soft figure-of-eight tie are reconstructed to demonstrate the book’s method.

generator.generation:
Create one full-bleed photorealistic TWO-PHOTO instructional sequence on one landscape 3:2 canvas (1536x1024 or same ratio). Split at its exact vertical midpoint with NO gutter, labels, frames, borders or other marks. Both resulting panels are 3:4 upright photographs. These are two images of the SAME actual Brussels sprout, photographed from precisely the same tripod position, distance and perspective a minute apart at John's real Cornish allotment. Their shared subject is the tall untidy plant on the left of his bed in the seed. Use the real camera pixels as closely as possible and make limited, natural edits. Identity of the plant, background and true gardening proportions are the priority. The old staged art is not the model.

INPUT 1: the same actual October video crop duplicated side by side as a registered starting plate. Use its panel framing as the basis for BOTH new halves. Lock the canopy contour, leaf positions, stem height and character, sky and real structures. The grass/clover path is on the LEFT and the dark soil under the plant; nearby brassicas remain behind the featured plant on the right. The distant stone/block boundary and the left-hand fragment of the neighbour's hoop frame and nearby roof are really there. Do not mirror or relocate anything. INPUT 2: close October camera view of the actual plant and timber. Young sprouts are small green buttons growing in the leaf axils on a real pale stem, irregular spacing, many long petioles still attached; ordinary crinkled, waxy broad leaves, a few yellowing lower leaves, some caterpillar holes, no need to prettify. No large round supermarket sprouts, unnaturally bare straight trunk, showroom crop, giant mallet or stage-set lighting. INPUT 3: genuine grass and exposed soil from the base of the same planting; use its texture when making the soil contacts visible. INPUT 4: A35/A43 are secondary surrounding allotment references only. Keep the actual October camera angle from input 1. INPUT 5: two older book diagrams show what the hands and tie are for. Use only mechanics; ignore drawn plant, art style, proportions and duplicated ties.

Keep the entire top of the foreground canopy where it is. Keep a clear vertical line on the ground at the bottom in both panels, with the rooted stem and the foot of the weathered square timber visibly entering the SAME ground, separated by a small gap. The stake stands to the right of the stem, as in the seed, at sensible distance just clear of the root crown. Remove the existing bright blue multi-plant ropes from this foreground stem and its stake in BOTH halves. Leave real leaf growth all through the stem. In both frames tuck JUST one or two nearby overlapping leaf stalks to the far side as needed, so a modest open window exposes (i) the stake top, (ii) a hand-width around the mid-stem tie area, and (iii) the soil and both bases. No clean vertical strip of bald plant. Put the same foliage and soil in the same places in the two panels. The base of the stake may be a little higher while being driven, as the same stake entering the same point, without any other scale or geometry changes.

LEFT panel, driving the stake. The sole new action is shown close and clearly. Two practical real hands and forearms come in from the RIGHT edge, no face or upper body. One hand holds the side of the squared weathered timber just below the striking point, fingers well clear. The other hand holds the handle of a modest, old wooden garden mallet. Its lower striking face is squarely aligned just above the real top of the post in mid-swing, with the head in a visible patch of air to the right of the crown, and handle leading to the right-hand grip. The mallet head is natural hand-tool size, about twice the post width. No tie around this plant yet. We can trace the separate bases at ground level and see the body of the stake in each image. Clear daylight, documentary colours.

RIGHT panel, finished. The SAME gardener and mallet have left the frame. A SINGLE soft pale blue-grey woven plant tie at mid-stem is the only new element. Its continuous physical path makes a loose SIDEWAYS FIGURE OF EIGHT with exactly one crossing in the open gap between stem and post. One complete gentle loop alone encircles the main green stalk, one complete loop alone encircles the wood at the same height. One band passes visibly over the other precisely BETWEEN them; neither crossing overlays the stem or overlaps the front of the stake. The right loop is tied off to the outer side of the post, with short unobtrusive ends. The loop around the plant has a sliver of air for thickening, the two individuals are held apart, and the broad soft matte tape can be visually followed even when small. Do not use cable ties, plastic buckle, rigid wire, bow with dangling ribbon, one common ring around both or extra loops around leaf stalks. Position the one tie in the clear window. Give gentle real shadows at the crossings.

Maintain the documentary look of an October frame: real ageing crop with natural asymmetry, same daylight, still camera, same grass strip and imperfect soil. The two photographs should feel like exposures on the same tripod and crop, with a readable distinct action in each. No typography, padding or diagram overlay.

Equal upright halves, zero gutters, no captions.
